narrative.question: How do I make this a routine that I and a teammate can repeat?
narrative.viewer_starts: A professional programmer who knows the shell, exit codes and echo $?, and has watched the changelog-entry skill measured through the course so far on two models (claude-haiku-4.5 and gpt-5.6-terra). Knows skill, eval file, stimulus, grader, trial, PASS, FAIL and ERROR, and the practice folder. Has four eval files: changelog (five single-request stimuli graded by patterns and a hidden script), conversation, loading, and wording (graded by an LLM judge with a rubric). Has used vally lint, vally oracle with a golden patch, vally grade to re-grade a saved run (it cannot re-grade script graders), vally eval with -e, --model, --runs, --workers and --output-dir, experiments (with-and-without, before-and-after), cost per passing trial in AIU (one AIU is about a cent), budget graders set to 215000 tokens, 10 turns and 30 seconds with the agent stopped after a minute, and vally compare with --fail-on-regression, whose pairwise judge exits 1 on a regression. Has four questions for a run that goes wrong, and knows an ERROR trial did not complete. Has never tagged a stimulus, defined a suite, or used --require-pass.

arc.viewer_can: choose the cheapest check that can answer the question in front of them
read a suite in .vally.yaml and predict the exit code of a run, with and without --require-pass
run a quick suite and a full suite so that a failing verdict or an over-budget trial is an error, and write the conventions down
keep the skill working after the next edit: say what the two suites and the page guard, what they cost, and what one trial per stimulus cannot show

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Keep it working' in the display serif. Three blocks in a row, no arrows: 'After every edit · one short command', 'Before sharing · a longer one', 'For the team · one page'. Each lights as the promise names it.
narration: Everything we've built works when we remember to run it, in the right order, with the right flags.
That isn't a routine, and it won't survive a busy week or a new teammate.
Meanwhile the skill will be edited again, and the models under it will change without telling us.
Here, you'll make the right check the easy one: one short command after every edit, a longer one before sharing, and one page that says what the team agreed.

scenes.on_screen: Eyebrow 'Cheapest check first'. Headline 'Five checks, cheapest first'. A row of five blocks, no arrows: lint · free, oracle · free, re-grade · free, quick · 10 runs, full · 30 runs. The three free ones light together, then quick, then full. A note: agent runs, for two models.
narration: Let's start with what each check costs.
We now have five ways to check the skill, and they differ enormously in cost.
Lint, the oracle and a re-grade start no agent, so for code graders they're free.
The other two are new here: a quick run of the stimuli that code can check, and a full run of everything.
On two models, the quick one spends ten agent runs, and the full one spends thirty.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Match the check to the question'. A table with three columns, Check, Answers, After: vally lint · is the eval file well formed · editing an eval file; vally oracle · do the graders pass a correct answer and fail an untouched file · changing a grader; vally grade · what do today's graders and budgets say about saved trials · changing a pattern, a budget or a rubric; quick · did the edit break what code can check, or go over budget · every edit to the skill; full · does everything still hold · before sharing, or a model change. Each row lights as it is named.
narration: The rule is to use the cheapest check that can answer the question we actually have.
After editing an eval file, that's lint.
After changing a grader, it's the oracle, which tries a correct answer and an untouched file.
After changing a pattern, a budget or a rubric, a re-grade says what the new version makes of trials already saved.
A script grader can't be re-graded, because the workspace it reads is gone.
So a change to a script goes back to the oracle.
After every edit to the skill, the quick run asks whether anything code can check has broken, or gone over budget.
Finally, before sharing the skill, or when a model changes, the full run asks whether everything still holds.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Three checks for one-off questions'. Three blocks, no arrows: 'With and without the skill · after a large rewrite', 'Before and after, then vally compare · did an edit help or hurt', 'Cost per passing trial · before changing model or effort'. Each lights in turn.
narration: Three more checks sit outside that order, because each answers a one-off question.
After a large rewrite, the with-and-without experiment says whether the skill still beats no skill.
To learn whether one edit really helped, we run a before-and-after experiment, then vally compare, which spends judge calls and starts no agent.
Finally, cost per passing trial is what to compare before moving to a different model or reasoning effort.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'What drifts is agreement'. Four blocks in a two-by-two grid, each a question: 'What deserves a grader?', 'Where do grading files go?', 'How is a result reported?', 'What may a run cost?'. Each lights as it is said. Under them a line: 'One page, written down while it is fresh'.
narration: For a team, though, the commands are the easy part.
What drifts is agreement: what deserves a grader, where grading files are kept, how a result is reported, and what a run may cost.
So we'll write those down on one page, while they're fresh.
People can disagree with something written down, and that's how the agreement gets better.

scenes.on_screen: Eyebrow 'Tags, suites and exit codes'. Headline 'A tag labels a stimulus'. File panel labelled 'evals/changelog.eval.yaml' with a minimap, showing the first three stimuli's name lines and the tags line under each, with a 'lines hidden' row between. One callout on the right: 'a name and a value · the words are ours'. The word tags lights, then 'tier: quick', then the same line under the next two stimuli.
narration: That's the plan; here's what Vally gives us to build it, starting with tags.
When we say tag, we mean a label on a stimulus: a name and a value, on a line named tags.
Here the name is tier and the value is quick; both words are ours, and any words will do.
All five stimuli in this file get the same line, because all five are graded by code.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'A suite names a group'. File panel labelled '.vally.yaml', the whole file (13 lines), with callouts on the right: 'the name we type' (quick), 'eval files it draws on', 'only stimuli tagged tier: quick' (filter), 'no filter: every stimulus' (full). Each lights as the voice reaches it.
narration: Next, the suite: a named group of stimuli.
It's a list of eval files, optionally narrowed to the stimuli with a given tag.
Suites are defined in a file named dot vally dot yaml, in the folder we run Vally from.
This one defines two; the first is named quick, which is what we'll type on the command line.
The quick suite draws on one eval file, and its filter is matched against each stimulus's tags, so it keeps the five we just tagged.
The second, full, lists four eval files with no filter, so every stimulus in them runs.
Those four hold the single requests, the conversation, the loading test, and the judged wording.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'One option runs a suite'. Dark box, left: the vally eval command over three lines, with '--suite quick' where '-e' and a file used to be. Callouts on the right: 'in place of -e and a file' beside --suite quick, 'as before' beside the model and workers lines.
narration: To run a suite, vally eval takes dash dash suite and the suite's name, in place of dash e and a file.
Everything else about the command works as before.
One thing to know: a suite only names stimuli, and adds no graders of its own.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Quick stimuli carry their budgets'. File panel labelled 'evals/changelog.eval.yaml' with a minimap, at the typo-fix stimulus: its constraints (max_agent_duration: 1m) and its three budget graders (token-budget 215000, turn-count 10, wall-time 30s). The panel scrolls to the three budgets as they are named and each lights in turn; then it scrolls back up to the time limit, which lights.
narration: The five quick stimuli are the ones that already have budgets, so the quick suite carries them.

narration.text: Every trial is checked against a ceiling on its tokens, on its turns, and on its time.

narration: The agent is also stopped after a minute, and whatever it had done by then is graded.
When a trial goes over a budget, its stimulus fails, exactly as it would for a wrong entry.
That's what makes the quick suite a cost check as well as a quality check.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Exit codes make failure loud'. A table: rows 'every stimulus passed', 'a stimulus failed', 'a trial ended in ERROR'; columns 'vally eval' (0, 0, 1) and 'with --require-pass' (0, 1, 1). The 'failed' row's first cell lights, then its second, then the ERROR row. A note: vally grade takes the same option.
narration: The last piece is the exit code, which is what scripts and automated checks act on.
Unless told otherwise, vally eval exits with zero even when stimuli fail, because the run itself completed.
Adding dash dash require pass changes that: any failing stimulus makes the exit code one, whichever grader failed it, budgets included.
When a trial ends in error, the exit code is one either way.
Vally grade accepts the same option.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'A third gate, for judged quality'. Dark box, left: the vally compare command over four lines (--baseline haiku-after, --treatment haiku-before, --judge-model, --fail-on-regression) and, under it, the mean-score line our run printed, then the mean-score and Regression lines of an earlier run. Callouts on the right: 'the newer skill' (baseline), 'the change under test' (treatment), 'exit 1 when the whole range is below zero', 'our run: exit 0', 'an earlier run: exit 1'.
narration: One kind of failure gets past every grader: an edit that makes the entries a little worse, while every pattern still matches.
That's what the pairwise judge is for.
Vally compare gives it two runs of the same stimuli, a baseline and a change, and it scores each pair of answers.
With dash dash fail on regression, the command exits with one when the change scored clearly worse.
Clearly worse means that the whole range around its score is below zero.

narration.text: Earlier, we tested it by treating the older skill as the change.
When we ran it, the range reached just above zero, so the command exited with zero.
In an earlier run of the same comparison, the whole range was below zero, and it exited with one.

narration: It needs a before-and-after experiment and about eighteen judge calls, so it belongs before we rely on an edit, not after every edit.
It also gates on the judged score alone; a rise in tokens is the budgets' job.

scenes.on_screen: Eyebrow 'Two suites and a conventions page'. Headline 'What would the exit code be?'. One block titled 'the quick suite, without --require-pass · one trial over its token budget, nothing else wrong'. After the question and a beat it opens into two parts: 'Exit code 0 · the run itself completed' and 'With --require-pass: 1 · a failing verdict becomes an error'.
narration: That's how the pieces work; now let's put them to work.
The tags and the suites file are in place in our practice folder, exactly as we just went through them.
Here's a question first: suppose we ran the quick suite without require pass, and one trial went over its token budget.

narration.text: Nothing else fails, and nothing errors: what would the exit code be?

narration: It would be zero: the budget fails that stimulus, but without the option, a failing verdict doesn't change the exit code.
So anything automated has to add the option, and we will too.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder; the prompt shows only the folder name. vally lint -e evals/changelog.eval.yaml prints its one warning. The screen is cleared out of sight. Then the quick suite over four lines (--suite quick, both models, --workers 2 --require-pass, --output-dir results/lesson-21-quick), a jump cut, the end of its output with the table, and echo $? printing the exit code. Held until read.

narration.text: First, we lint the eval file, since we've just edited it.
There's one warning, the usual one about scoring defaults, and no errors.
Now the quick suite, on both models, two workers at a time, with require pass so that a failure is an error.
Its results go to a folder of their own, and it spends ten agent runs.
The table at the end counts the stimuli that passed, out of five, for each model.
About a minute later, every stimulus has passed on both models, budgets included.
So what was its exit code?
Zero: nothing failed.

scenes.chapter: See a failure exit with one
scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder. cd into the one run folder under results/lesson-5-before (its name completed with Tab); then vally grade over two lines with --run-dir . --require-pass, reading results.jsonl; its blocks scroll, ending on the last ones; then echo $? prints 1. Held until read.

narration.text: A passing run can't show the option at work, so let's see a wrong entry fail loudly, without spending anything.
The run we'll use is the first one we graded, before the skill had its rules, so it has plenty of failures.
None of its graders is a script, and a script grader is the one kind that can't be re-graded.
We change into that run's folder.
Then we re-grade it with today's eval file, and with require pass.
These are the failing blocks from that run, each now with the budgets among its graders.
Every budget passed in all eighteen trials, three stimuli three times on two models; only the graders of the result failed.
So what's the exit code this time?
It's one: a failing verdict is now an error.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'One budget lowered, for a moment'. File panel labelled 'evals/changelog.eval.yaml' with a minimap, at the typo-fix stimulus's token-budget grader, whose max now reads 70000. A callout: 'was 215000'. The max line lights.
narration: Next, a trial that's over budget, which none of ours is, so we make one for a moment.

narration.text: In the typo fix stimulus, we lower the token budget from two hundred fifteen thousand to seventy thousand, which is below what those trials used.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the run's folder. The same vally grade command with --require-pass; its blocks scroll; then echo $? prints 1. Held until read.

narration.text: We run the same re-grade again, and then print the exit code.
It's one again.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Over budget fails like any other'. Dark box, left: one typo-fix block from that re-grade as printed (4/5 graders passed; token-budget max 70000, the trial's tokens exceed it; Score 98.8% | FAILED). Callouts on the right: 'did the work' (4/5), 'cost too much' (the budget line), 'the score decides nothing here' (the score line). A note gives the other trials' token counts.
narration: That output is longer than one screen, so here's the part that changed.

narration.text: These typo fix trials passed every grader a moment ago; now they fail, on the budget alone.
Seventy-four thousand tokens is over a maximum of seventy thousand.
The score still says ninety-eight point eight percent.

narration: That's because going slightly over a budget costs only a little of the score.
With no scoring block, though, the score decides nothing: every grader has to pass, and one didn't.
So a trial that did the work and cost too much is a failing verdict like any other.
With that seen, the budget goes back to two hundred fifteen thousand.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder. The full suite over four lines (--suite full, both models, --workers 2 --require-pass, --output-dir results/lesson-21-full), a jump cut, then the end of its output: the model summary and the table with a row per eval file, every cell passing; then echo $? prints 0. Held until read.

narration.text: Now everything, once: the full suite, with the same options, into its own results folder.
It spends thirty agent runs and six judge calls.
The table at the end has a row for each of the four eval files.
Several minutes later, every stimulus has passed on both models, in all four files.
Let's see what it reported.
Zero again: nothing failed, budgets and judge included.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Our first run had trouble'. Left: the table of our FIRST run of the full suite (eval file, one column per model, passed of total). Right: two cards: 'ERROR × 2 · conversation · three-requests and wording · cache on claude-haiku-4.5 · Session disconnected' and 'FAIL · loading · skip-question on gpt-5.6-terra · the skill loaded for a question that should not load it'. A note: our first run, minutes before the one we kept, exit code 1. The ERROR card lights, then the FAIL card.

narration.text: That was our second run of the full suite; the first, a few minutes before it, ended differently.
Here's the first run's table, with the three stimuli Vally listed above it.
They're two different kinds of trouble.
On haiku, two trials ended in error, because their sessions dropped.

narration: As before, an error isn't a verdict: the trial didn't complete, so it says nothing about the skill.

narration.text: So we ran the suite again, and that's the run we kept.
The other is a real fail: on terra, a question that shouldn't load the skill did load it.
The loading grader that forbids that is what caught it.
Either problem alone makes the command exit with one, and that first run did.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Ten headings, one page'. File panel labelled 'CONVENTIONS.md' with a minimap. It opens at the first headings and scrolls down through the page in steps, as the voice names them; the last heading, 'Models and dates', lights at the end.
narration: One thing is left: the page that says what we've agreed.
Ours is a file named conventions, with ten headings and a sentence or two under each.
It opens with what earns a grader, code before judge, where files are kept, and what we check before trusting a grader or a judge.
Then come what we run and when, how we report a result, and what a run may cost.
The last two are what to do when a run goes wrong, and which models we used, on which date.
That last one matters because models and their prices change: a result means little without knowing which model produced it, and when.

scenes.on_screen: Eyebrow 'Where the skill stands'. Headline 'From one pair to two suites'. Three blocks in a row, no arrows: 'At the start · a first draft, and a tick that hid a made-up number', 'First graders · 1 of 6 pairs passed', '30 of 30 · stimuli passed on each model, in the full suite'. Each lights in turn.
narration: So where does the skill stand?
At the start, it was a first draft that one model answered by making up a pull request number, behind a tick that hid it.

narration.text: With our first graders, one pair of stimulus and model passed, out of six.

narration: Now the suites cover a conversation, a loading test with near-miss requests, a judged quality that no pattern can see, and budgets on every quick stimulus.

narration.text: In our last run, every stimulus in them passed on both models.

narration: Every rule in the skill is there because a trial showed it was needed, and every grader is there because a failure was seen.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'What the routine costs'. A table: rows 'quick suite' and 'full suite'; columns trials, AIU, about (dollars). Under it a line with the largest quick trial's tokens beside the budget. The quick row lights, then the full row, then the tokens line. A note names the run.
narration: Now, what does the routine cost?

narration.text: In our run, the quick suite's ten trials cost about twenty-four AIU, which is about twenty-four cents an edit.
The full suite's thirty trials cost about sixty-seven AIU, with its six judge calls on top.
None of the quick trials came near the token budget: the largest used ninety-one thousand tokens, against two hundred fifteen thousand.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'A cheaper model, checked first'. Two blocks side by side: 'our two models · about 24 AIU an edit' and 'claude-haiku-5.5, low effort · about 1 AIU an edit · 15 of 15 passed earlier'. Under them, three numbered steps from the conventions: compare cost per passing trial; re-test the budgets on its saved trials; run the full suite on it first. Each lights as it is said.
narration: Those figures are for the two models we've used throughout.

narration.text: Earlier, in the cost experiment, the newer haiku model at low effort passed all fifteen of its trials on these same stimuli, at about a fifth of an AIU each.
On that one variant, a quick suite would cost about one AIU an edit: a cent.

narration: Our conventions say how to make that move: compare cost per passing trial, re-test the budgets on its saved trials, and run the full suite on it first.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'One trial per stimulus'. Two blocks side by side for the loading question skip-question on terra: '0 of 1 · in our first run' and '1 of 1 · in the second run, minutes later'. Under them: 'One pass shows it can pass, not that it will every time.' The first block lights, then the second.
narration: One caution goes with that last table: it's one trial per stimulus.

narration.text: In our two runs of the full suite, the same loading question failed on terra the first time, and passed the second.

narration: A single passing trial shows that a stimulus can pass; it doesn't show that it will pass every time.
The suites are how we find out when that changes.

scenes.on_screen: Eyebrow 'Recap'. Headline 'What are the five checks?'. One block, 'cheapest check first', which opens after the question and a pause into five parts, each lit as it is said: lint · after editing an eval file; oracle · after changing a grader; re-grade · after changing a pattern, budget or rubric; quick suite · after every edit; full suite · before sharing, or a model change.
narration: Before you go on: what are the five checks, from cheapest to most expensive?

narration.text: Lint, after editing an eval file.

narration: The oracle, after changing a grader.
Re-grading a saved run, after changing a pattern, a budget or a rubric.
The quick suite, after every edit to the skill.
Finally, the full suite, before sharing, and whenever a model changes.

scenes.on_screen: 'Next' card. Headline 'The skill inside an app' in the display serif. Below: 'Start the agent where the app would: does the skill hold when an app, not a person, starts the agent?' A note: 'Exercises and the workflow guide are on the course site · Source: Vally docs, Authoring Eval Suites'.
narration: That completes the first part of the course.
You can now run a quick suite after every edit and a full suite before sharing, with commands that fail loudly on a failing verdict, an over-budget trial, or a regression.
You also have a one-page conventions file to hand to a teammate.
In the second part, the team behind our made-up tool has put the skill inside its release tooling.
Does it still hold when an app, not a person, starts the agent?
That's the next lesson.
The exercises on the lesson page are worth doing first, and the workflow guide there shows how a service can run the quick suite on every proposed change.
